bat-removal.intro: Gadsden is rural Richland County — a small farming community south of Columbia, a short drive from the Congaree swamp, where big old farmhouses stand on generous lots under mature oaks. Its bat colonies are correspondingly grand: little brown and big brown bats in the tall, undisturbed attic voids of houses that have stood for a century, feeding over the farm fields and the creek branches that run to the Congaree. A Gadsden colony is often an old one — guano measured in years, entries polished by generations of wings — and it is usually discovered by the staining on the gable or the smell in a closed-up room, not by noise.
bat-removal.extendedBody:
Century houses and established colonies

Excluding an established colony from a Gadsden farmhouse is a mapping exercise. A roofline that has been in service for a hundred years offers bats a dozen candidate gaps — eave returns, chimney flashing, the junctions of every addition — and the colony uses several. We read the staining and flight lines to find the active exits, fit one-way devices there when the timing is right, and seal every secondary gap in the same programme. Timing follows SCDNR guidance rather than a statute — South Carolina sets no fixed bat dates — because sealing a maternity colony while pups are flightless fails and is cruel; colonies found in early summer are mapped and scheduled. The guano load in an old colony's attic is assessed honestly as part of the work: years of accumulation is a cleanup conversation, and we will have it with photographs rather than adjectives, so an owner — including one who has inherited the house and the colony together — can decide with the evidence in front of them.

faqs.q: We inherited a Gadsden farmhouse and found years of bat guano in the attic. Where do we start?
faqs.a: With the colony, then the cleanup — in that order, because cleaning an occupied attic just refurnishes the roost. We inspect and map the colony's entries, exclude the bats in the proper window, and seal the roofline completely. Then the guano: we will show you photographs and a measured assessment of what is up there, and quote the removal and sanitation separately and plainly. Long-established farmhouse colonies are common around the Congaree side of the county; a house that has stood quiet for a century is exactly the roost bats select, and none of it is a reflection on the house — only on how long it has been available.

faqs.q: How much does bat removal cost in Gadsden?
faqs.a: It depends on the colony's size and the roofline's entry count — the big farmhouses run larger because they present more gaps and hold older colonies. We inspect first and quote the complete exclusion firmly, with any attic cleanup quoted separately and only if the inspection shows it is warranted. If pups are flightless when we find the colony, the mapping is done immediately and the exclusion is scheduled for the right window at the quoted price.

dead-animal-removal.intro: Dead-animal calls in Gadsden follow the farm calendar and the housing stock: big old farmhouses with deep wall voids and crawlspaces, barns and outbuildings on every parcel, and fields and woods on all sides. The typical case is the smell that arrives three days after the scratching stopped — a raccoon or opossum that got into a wall void or under the floor and could not get out, or an animal that died in the crawlspace over the winter and announced itself in the first warm week. On farm properties there is a second category: animals dead in barns, well houses, and feed rooms, where the removal is also a sanitation question for the animals that are supposed to be there.
dead-animal-removal.extendedBody:
Finding it is the job

In dead-animal work the removal is the easy half; the location is the craft. Odour travels through a farmhouse's voids in ways that mislead — the strongest smell in a room is often a room away from the carcass, carried by the crawlspace air. We work from the evidence: the last scratching the household heard, the fly activity at the vents, the staining, and the structure's own map of voids. Crawlspaces under Gadsden's pier-built homes are searched completely, not sampled, and wall voids are opened at the carcass, not at the guess. What we remove, we bag and take away, and the void is treated so the smell clears in days rather than weeks. Then the honest part of the visit: how it got in. A dead raccoon in a wall void arrived through a live entry, and that entry is still open — we identify it and quote the exclusion on the spot, because the alternative is meeting again over the next animal that uses the same door and makes the same mistake.

faqs.q: There is a strong dead smell in our Gadsden home but we cannot find anything. Can you locate it?
faqs.a: That is the normal shape of the call — the carcass is almost always in a void: a wall, the crawlspace, a chimney, or the duct run. We locate by evidence rather than by opening walls at random: fly activity, the smell's behaviour through the day, and the house's void map. Most are found within the first inspection, removed the same visit, and the void treated. We will also show you the entry the animal used, because in an older farmhouse there is always one, and sealing it is the difference between a one-time call and a recurring one.

faqs.q: How much does dead animal removal cost in Gadsden?
faqs.a: It depends on access — a carcass in an open crawlspace is a short job; one in a sealed wall void that has to be located by evidence and opened precisely is longer. We give you the price before we open anything, once the location is confirmed or narrowed to a void we can stand behind. The visit includes the entry inspection: if the animal got in alive through a gap, we quote that fix separately and plainly, with no obligation attached to it.
